CIBINETIDE / ARA-290

A tissue-protective peptide with something unusual in the biohacking world: controlled human evidence tied to neuropathy—and signals of nerve-fiber repair.

Cibinetide, originally known as ARA-290, is an 11-amino-acid peptide engineered from erythropoietin biology to activate a tissue-protective repair pathway without stimulating red-blood-cell production. Small randomized human trials in sarcoidosis-associated small-fiber neuropathy and type 2 diabetes have produced intriguing symptom and nerve-fiber signals.

In Plain English

Cibinetide is designed to switch on the body’s tissue-protection and repair signaling without the blood-building effects of erythropoietin, making it especially interesting for nerve damage, neuropathic symptoms and inflammation.

Editorial verdict
Real human neuropathy signal.
Still investigational.

This is more than a mechanistic peptide story: randomized human studies exist. The evidence remains relatively small and disease-specific, and cibinetide is not an FDA-approved treatment.

Ratings are editorial orientation and should be read alongside the studied disease populations, endpoints, sample sizes and regulatory status.
01 / WHAT IT IS

Erythropoietin biology—without trying to make more red blood cells.

Cibinetide is an 11-amino-acid peptide derived from the three-dimensional structure of erythropoietin and designed to activate tissue-protective signaling rather than erythropoiesis.

The research describes this pathway as an “innate repair receptor” involved in cytoprotection, modulation of inflammation and tissue repair. That mechanism has made cibinetide especially interesting in conditions involving small nerve fibers and inflammatory injury.

02 / HUMAN EVIDENCE

This is not just an animal-model story.

A 2012 randomized double-blind pilot trial enrolled 22 people with sarcoidosis and symptoms of small-fiber neuropathy. Cibinetide improved the Small Fiber Neuropathy Screening List score versus placebo at four weeks. Pain measured by the Brief Pain Inventory improved in both groups rather than showing a clear drug-placebo separation.

A subsequent blinded placebo-controlled study reported improvement in neuropathic symptoms along with increased corneal nerve-fiber density and changes in sensory and functional measures. In a later Phase 2b trial of 64 subjects, the 4 mg group showed a statistically significant placebo-corrected increase in corneal nerve-fiber area; pain improved in all groups.

Why this is interesting: some of the human signal is structural—not only subjective pain reporting. Corneal and skin nerve-fiber measures create a plausible disease-modification hypothesis that deserves larger confirmation.
03 / DIABETIC NEUROPATHY

A second human population produced another signal.

A Phase 2 study in people with type 2 diabetes and painful neuropathy reported improvements in neuropathic symptoms and metabolic measures during and after a 28-day treatment period.

The investigators also reported a nerve-fiber signal: participants starting with reduced corneal nerve-fiber density showed an increase compared with placebo. The study was exploratory and relatively small, so these findings are better treated as evidence supporting further clinical development than as definitive efficacy.

04 / COMMUNITY SIGNAL

The community is extending a neuropathy story into a broader repair story.

Interest around ARA-290 increasingly centers on nerve pain, nerve recovery, inflammation and tissue repair.

Unlike many emerging compounds, that interest has a recognizable clinical foundation: neuropathy was actually studied in humans. The stretch occurs when disease-specific findings are generalized to unrelated nerve injuries, musculoskeletal recovery or broad systemic “healing.”

Our read: this is exactly where Community Signal can be useful. Reports outside the studied populations may reveal hypotheses worth testing—but they should remain visibly distinct from the sarcoidosis and diabetic-neuropathy evidence.
05 / CLAIM VS EVIDENCE

One of the narrower gaps in the emerging-peptide world.

“ARA-290 has human neuropathy data.”Supported. Multiple controlled studies have evaluated cibinetide in small-fiber neuropathy populations.
“It may support nerve repair.”There is an intriguing human signal: studies reported changes in corneal and skin small nerve-fiber measures. Larger confirmatory trials are still needed.
“It is proven for neuropathic pain.”Too strong. Symptom findings are encouraging but not uniformly separated from placebo across pain endpoints.
“It heals any nerve injury.”Not established. Evidence from disease-associated small-fiber neuropathy cannot automatically be generalized to radiculopathy, traumatic nerve injury or other neurologic conditions.
“It is an FDA-approved regenerative peptide.”No. Cibinetide remains investigational and is not an FDA-approved drug.
06 / THE GAP

MODERATE

Clinical Evidence × Community Signal
MODERATE

For small-fiber neuropathy, the gap is narrower than it is for many peptides in the Index because controlled human studies include symptoms and objective nerve-fiber measures. The gap widens considerably when cibinetide is positioned as a general treatment for nerve injury, pain, inflammation or recovery.

07 / SAFETY + REGULATORY

Investigational—and not supported for 503A compounding.

Cibinetide is not an FDA-approved drug. FDA's Substance Registration System recognizes Cibinetide, ARA-290 and ARA290 as names for the same substance, but FDA explicitly notes that a UNII identifier does not imply regulatory review or approval.

FDA's 503A bulks-list materials place Cibinetide (ARA-290) in Category 3: substances nominated without adequate support for evaluation. That is a compounding-status classification, not an assessment that the published human research is invalid.

The clinical safety signal so far is encouraging but limited. Early controlled trials reported no major safety signal, but relatively small short-duration studies cannot define long-term or broad-population safety.
